title: One sub-plan's answer feeds another
idea: Composing functions: the value RETURNED by one sub-plan becomes the ARGUMENT to another. Build bigger answers from smaller ones.

exercises.prompt:
Read:

def double(n):
    return n * 2

def add_one(n):
    return n + 1

print(add_one(double(5)))

Which call runs FIRST?
options: double(5) — the inner call runs first
They run at the same time
exercises.explanation: The inner call runs first: double(5) becomes 10. Then add_one(10) runs. Inside-out, like any nested expression.
double(5) is 10; add_one(10) is 11. The returned 10 became the input to add_one.

exercises.prompt: Because a call becomes a value, you can put one call INSIDE another call's parentheses.
exercises.explanation: Yes. double(5) is a value (10), so it can sit where add_one expects an argument. That's composing.

exercises.prompt: Why does composing only work with RETURNING sub-plans (not printing ones)?
options: The inner call must hand back a value to feed the outer call
exercises.explanation: The outer call needs a value as its argument. Only return hands one back; a printing sub-plan would feed None.
Inner first (10), outer next (11), then print shows 11. Always resolve the innermost call first.
double(3) is 6; add_one(6) is 7. The inner call's returned value feeds the outer one.

exercises.prompt: REVIEW: in add_one(double(5)), double's returned value acts as...
exercises.explanation: The returned value is passed as add_one's argument. Returning + passing arguments is what makes composing possible.

exercises.prompt: Composing lets you build a bigger answer by chaining small, reusable sub-plans.
exercises.explanation: Exactly. Each sub-plan does one small job; feeding one into the next builds up to the full answer.

exercises.prompt: Arrange a program that composes: define double, define add_one, then print add_one(double(4)).
exercises.explanation: Define both sub-plans first, then compose them in one line: double(4)->8, add_one(8)->9.

exercises.prompt: The big idea of this unit:
options: A sub-plan's returned value can become the input to another — composing
exercises.explanation: Compose sub-plans: the inner one hands back a value that feeds the outer one. Small pieces, bigger answers.
